newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Czech PM briefs EU on austerity measures.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM briefs EU on austerity measures.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus on Tuesday briefed the European Commission on a fiscal and monetary austerity package aimed at bringing the economy back on track.
Klaus declined to give any details, but told journalists the measures would be unveiled in Prague on Wednesday after they were put before a meeting of the full cabinet.
"They (the measures) represent an important shift in the completion of the transformation of the Czech Republic towards EU membership," Klaus said after the meeting.

He added that he believed he had succeeded in convincing the European Commission of the determination of the Czech Republic to meet the requirements set out for his country to open full membership talks with the EU early next year.

The measures are expected to include steep spending cuts, curbs on public sector wages, possible quotas on some imports and help for exporters, a tightening of tax loopholes and a new privatisation drive.
The package, which independent economists say could save up to $1 billion is critical to restoring foreign confidence in the country, dented by a swelling trade deficit and high interest rates.
A Commission report recently predicted the country's trade deficit for 1996 would soar to $5.8 billion, compared to $3.7 billion in 1995.
It said this resulted from the continuing strength of imports -- growing at 35 percent compared to export growth in dollar terms of 29 percent for the period from January to November.
Klaus, a free-market advocate, says his country has no alternative to full EU membership and has vowed to take any necessary action to bring the current account deficit back on track.
At the moment it is set to reach some seven percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) compared to three percent in 1995.
Earlier, Klaus met Jose Cutileiro, the secretary-general of the European Union's emerging defence body, the Western European Union (WEU), for talks on European defence issues.
The Czech Republic is also leading the field for quick admission to the WEU and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- the West's other two main democratic institutions.

NATO is set to invite new members to join the military alliance at a special summit in Madrid next July. EU membership will not take place until after the turn of the century, but Prague is keen to begin negotiations.

Those negotiations will not start until after a review by existing member governments of the EU's founding treaties this summer which may also bring the WEU into a closer permanent relationship with the European Union.
